summary: This meta-analysis by Heishman, Kleykamp and Singleton reviews 41 double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory studies (1994–2008) of nicotine and smoking effects on human performance in healthy adult nonsmokers or non-deprived smokers. Across nine performance domains, nicotine or smoking significantly improved six: fine motor, alerting attention (accuracy and RT), orienting attention (RT), short-term episodic memory (accuracy), and working memory (RT), with effect sizes from 0.16 to 0.44. The authors conclude these gains are likely true performance enhancement rather than withdrawal relief, with implications for smoking initiation and tobacco dependence maintenance.
one_line: A 2010 meta-analysis of 41 placebo-controlled studies finding nicotine and smoking significantly enhance fine motor skills, attention, and memory in non-deprived adults.
key_facts: The meta-analysis was published in Psychopharmacology (Berl) in July 2010, volume 210, issue 4, pages 453–469.
The authors were Stephen J. Heishman, Bethea A. Kleykamp, and Edward G. Singleton.
The meta-analysis included 41 double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory studies published from 1994 to 2008.
Participants were healthy adult nonsmokers or smokers who were not tobacco-deprived or were minimally deprived (≤2 h).
Sufficient effect size data existed to conduct meta-analyses on nine performance domains.

Nicotine or smoking had significant positive effects on six domains: fine motor, alerting attention-accuracy and response time (RT), orienting attention-RT, short-term episodic memory-accuracy, and working memory-RT.
The reported effect size range for significant domains was 0.16 to 0.44.
The review updated a previous review by Heishman et al. published in Exp Clin Psychopharmacol 2:345–395, 1994.
The authors argue the effects on motor abilities, attention, and memory likely represent true performance enhancement because they are not confounded by withdrawal relief.
The authors state the beneficial cognitive effects of nicotine have implications for initiation of smoking and maintenance of tobacco dependence.
Empirical studies indicate nicotine enhances some aspects of attention and cognition, suggesting a role in maintaining tobacco dependence.
The article's PMID is 20414766 and its PMCID is PMC3151730.
The keywords include nicotine, tobacco, smoking, performance, motor, attention, memory, cognition, smokers, and nonsmokers.
